**Audience**: an engineer who has already compared two histograms (KL, MMD) and seen domain adaptation "work on a toy, die in prod".

**Empirical first**: EMD too slow on 5k points; Sinkhorn diverging when $\varepsilon$ is too small; FID dropping while the eye sees no gain — then we name Monge, Wasserstein, duality.

Theory (Monge, Kantorovich, duality) + practice (Sinkhorn / POT), then losses, domain adaptation, Gromov-Wasserstein and fairness. Flamary & Gaucher (CMAP); Flamary co-created POT.

### What you will be able to do

-   Formulate Monge's transport problem and its Kantorovich relaxation, and relate them to linear programming.
-   Exploit duality to interpret the Wasserstein distance and its potentials.
-   Implement the Sinkhorn algorithm and understand the role of entropic regularization.
-   Use transport as a machine learning tool: Wasserstein losses, domain adaptation, barycenters.
-   Understand Gromov-Wasserstein to compare objects with no direct correspondence, typically graphs.
-   Apply transport to fairness questions, acting on distributions rather than on predictions.

### Course outline

-   **Review: convexity and LP duality** — the two reading keys for the rest of the module.
-   **The transport problem** — from Monge to Kantorovich: moving mass at minimum cost, and why we relax.
-   **Duality and the Wasserstein distance** — the dual viewpoint, and the geometry the distance induces on distributions.
-   **Entropic regularization: Sinkhorn** — making transport computable, iteration by iteration.
-   **OT and machine learning** — Wasserstein losses, domain adaptation, barycenters: the toolbox in action.
-   **Gromov-Wasserstein and beyond** — transporting between spaces with no correspondence, up to the FGW and COOT variants.
-   **Fairness through transport** — correcting distributional disparities between populations.
-   **Research at CMAP (Flamary, Gaucher)** — a tour of the research work of Rémi Flamary (self-study, and entry points for the project).
-   **Exercises** and **References** — systematic training and sources to go further.

### How to study this module

-   First absorb convexity and duality (the review section): almost every theorem of the course is a duality theorem in disguise.
-   Solve tiny discrete cases by hand (two or three points): the optimal transport plan takes shape there, and the intuition generalizes.
-   Experiment with the POT library, created by the instructor: varying the entropic regularization and observing the transport plan is the best way to understand Sinkhorn.
-   Relate each application to the generic problem "compare two distributions": a loss, domain adaptation or fairness are just different instances of this same question.
-   Read the Wasserstein-GAN (proposition 4.2) and the Bures formula behind the FID (theorem 2.7) as complete applications: they are proved here and need no other course. Multimodal Generative AI, an alternative to this module in the same choose-1 group, uses them as tools; its pages are optional reading.
-   Redo the exercises of each section before moving on to the next; the hand calculations prepare the software implementation.

::: note
[independent note]{.tag} Cross-cutting language: the FID of generative-model evaluation (theorem 2.7), graph alignment (Gromov-Wasserstein → M2), fairness. A differentiator in data science / research — if you know *when* Sinkhorn is enough and when exact EMD is a trap.
:::

## 0. Review: convexity and LP duality {#ch0}

Every transport problem of this course is a convex optimization problem, and most of its proofs are duality arguments. This review states the four tools used throughout: linear-programming duality, the pushforward of a measure, uniqueness under strict convexity, and the positivity of the Kullback-Leibler divergence.

:::: recap
::: recap-title
L3 background used
:::

-   **Convex sets and functions**: for convex $f$, any stationary point is a global minimum; for *strictly* convex $f$, the minimizer (if it exists) is **unique** — entropic OT in ch. 3 takes advantage of this;
-   **Linear programming**: minimize $c^\top x$ subject to $Ax = b$, $x \geq 0$;
-   **Measure theory**: probability, expectation $\mathbb{E}_\mu[f] = \int f\,d\mu$, pushforward measure;
-   **Entropy**: Kullback-Leibler divergence, Jensen's inequality — the engine of entropic regularization.
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 0.1 — LP duality: weak (proved), strong, complementarity (proved)]{.tag} Primal (left) and dual (right):
$$
\min\{c^\top x \ : \ Ax = b,\ x \geq 0\}, \qquad \max\{b^\top y \ : \ A^\top y \leq c\}.
$$

-   **Weak duality**: for any pair of feasible points, $c^\top x \geq b^\top y$.
-   **Strong duality**: if the primal is feasible and bounded, the dual attains its optimum and the values coincide.
-   **Complementarity**: at the optima $x^\star, y^\star$: $x^\star_j > 0 \Rightarrow (A^\top y^\star)_j = c_j$.

::: proof
**Weak duality.** Summing the dual constraints weighted by $x_j \geq 0$,
$$
c^\top x \geq (A^\top y)^\top x = y^\top (Ax) = y^\top b .
$$

**Strong duality.** Admitted (polyhedron separation).

**Complementarity.** At the optimum,
$$
0 = c^\top x^\star - b^\top y^\star = (c - A^\top y^\star)^\top x^\star = \sum_j \underbrace{(c - A^\top y^\star)_j}_{\geq 0}\, \underbrace{x^\star_j}_{\geq 0} .
$$
Every term is zero, hence the implication.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.2 — Pushforward measure and transfer lemma (proved)]{.tag} For measurable $T : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d$, the **pushforward measure** gives to each set $A$ "the mass of what is sent into $A$":
$$
T_\#\mu(A) = \mu\big(T^{-1}(A)\big).
$$
**Transfer lemma**: for every positive or bounded measurable $f$,
$$
\int f\,d(T_\#\mu) = \int f \circ T\,d\mu.
$$

::: proof
For $f = \mathbf{1}_A$ this is the definition. Both sides are linear in $f$: the equality passes to positive simple functions, then to all positive functions by monotone convergence, then to bounded ones by taking differences. This "moving the change of variables into the measure" is used on every page of this course.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.3 — Strict convexity: uniqueness (proved)]{.tag} If a strictly convex $F$ attains its minimum at $x^\star$, then $x^\star$ is the unique minimizer.

::: proof
If $x \neq x^\star$ were also a minimizer, the midpoint $m = \tfrac12(x + x^\star)$ would give $F(m) < \tfrac12F(x) + \tfrac12F(x^\star) = \min F$ — a contradiction.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.4 — KL ≥ 0 (proved by Gibbs/Jensen), with equality case]{.tag} For discrete distributions $p, q$ (or densities): $$\mathrm{KL}(p \| q) = \sum_i p_i \log\frac{p_i}{q_i} \ \geq\ 0, \qquad \text{equality} \iff p = q.$$

::: proof
By definition,
$$
\mathrm{KL}(p\|q) = -\sum_i p_i \log\frac{q_i}{p_i} .
$$
The $\log$ function is concave: by Jensen *weighted by $p$* (Gibbs' inequality),
$$
\sum_i p_i \log\frac{q_i}{p_i} \leq \log\sum_i p_i\frac{q_i}{p_i} = \log\sum_i q_i = 0 .
$$
Equality in Jensen (strict concavity of $\log$) requires $q_i/p_i$ constant on $\{p_i > 0\}$, and the constant equals 1 because both are probabilities.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

## 1. The transport problem {#ch1}

Concrete scene: two 1D histograms of 20 bins each, a source and a target. A greedy coupling that sends each bin to the nearest bin with remaining capacity costs 12.4; the linear-programming solver of POT finds 7.1.

And when one source bin must feed two target bins, no deterministic map can do the job, whereas a transport plan that splits the mass exists. This chapter states the two formulations of the problem, Monge's and Kantorovich's, before any algorithm.

::: note
[What breaks]{.tag} Demanding a Monge map when mass must split; dropping marginal constraints (it is no longer transport); over-regularizing (plan too blurry, metric useless). All three sabotage domain adaptation as much as a 3-point toy.
:::

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Monge's problem (1781)]{.tag} Given two probability measures $\mu, \nu$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$ and a cost $c(x, y)$ (typically $\|x - y\|^2$), find a transport map $T : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d$ that moves the first measure onto the second while minimizing the total cost.

In other words, $T_\#\mu = \nu$ and $T$ solves
$$
\min_T \ \int c\big(x, T(x)\big)\, d\mu(x).
$$

Historical note: cut and fill (Monge, 1781); the problem is *non-convex* in $T$, and a solution may not exist.
:::

::: ex
[Example 1.2 — Non-existence of a Monge map: 1 to 2 (detailed)]{.tag} Take $\mu = \delta_0$ (unit mass at the origin) and $\nu = \tfrac12\delta_{-1} + \tfrac12\delta_{+1}$ (two half-masses).

A map $T$ sends 0 to *a single point* $T(0)$, so the pushforward measure is **atomic at a single point**:
$$
T_\#\delta_0 = \delta_{T(0)} .
$$
It is impossible to obtain $\nu$, which has two.

The mass must be "split": the random pair $(X, Y)$ with $X = 0$ and $Y = \pm1$ by a coin flip realizes the transport, but a map does not. This is exactly what Kantorovich formalizes: allowing splitting.
:::

:::: thm
[Kantorovich's formulation (1942) — the pivot of the course]{.tag} Relax "each source goes to a single destination" into a transport plan $\gamma$ — the law of a pair $(X, Y)$ with marginals $\mu, \nu$:

::: key
[Key result — Kantorovich's problem]{.tag}
$$
W_c(\mu, \nu) \;=\; \min_{\gamma \in \Pi(\mu, \nu)} \ \int c(x, y)\, d\gamma(x, y),
$$
$$
\Pi(\mu,\nu) = \big\{\gamma \geq 0 \ :\ \gamma(\cdot \times \mathbb{R}^d) = \mu,\ \gamma(\mathbb{R}^d \times \cdot) = \nu\big\}.
$$
:::

**Discrete case** ($\mu = \sum_i a_i \delta_{x_i}$, $\nu = \sum_j b_j \delta_{y_j}$, $\mathbf{1}^\top a = \mathbf{1}^\top b = 1$): a **linear program** on the transport matrix $\Gamma$,
$$
\min_{\Gamma \in \mathbb{R}_+^{n \times m}} \ \langle C, \Gamma\rangle \quad \text{s.t.} \quad \Gamma \mathbf{1} = a,\ \Gamma^\top \mathbf{1} = b,
$$
where $C_{ij} = c(x_i, y_j)$.
::::

::: thm
[Theorem 1.3 — Existence (by compactness) and structure of solutions]{.tag}

-   $\Pi(\mu,\nu)$ is a **non-empty convex compact** (discrete: a bounded polytope defined by closed constraints; general: compactness in the sense of narrow convergence, by tightness). The cost being continuous, the minimum is **attained** (Weierstrass).
-   **Extreme solutions**: there exists an optimal solution that is a vertex of the polytope, and such a vertex has at most $n + m - 1$ non-zero coefficients.

    *Proof (sketch)*: the $n + m$ equality constraints are dependent (the sum of the row constraints equals that of the columns: rank $\leq n + m - 1$). A vertex of a polyhedron in dimension $nm$ is defined by $nm$ independent active constraints, of which at least $nm - (n+m-1)$ are bounds $\Gamma_{ij} = 0$.
:::

::: note
[Why the relaxation is "lossless"]{.tag} Example 1.2 shows it is sometimes *necessary* (mass splitting). It is also *sufficient* in the sense that, as soon as $\mu$ has a density with respect to Lebesgue (the case of all data clouds), the optimal Kantorovich plan is **induced by a map** $T$: $\gamma^\star = (\mathrm{Id}, T)_\#\mu$ — this is Brenier's theorem, proved in ch. 2.

In the discrete case, on the other hand ($n$ sources, $m$ targets), the vertices with $\leq n+m-1$ non-zeros are "almost" deterministic — how much splitting remains is the subject of exercise 8. Logistic interpretation: mines and coke ovens (Hitchcock, Kantorovich) — nowadays, comparing two data distributions.
:::

## 2. Duality and the Wasserstein distance {#ch2}

Computing a transport plan is a minimization; its dual, a maximization over pairs of potentials, gives certificates of optimality, the structure of optimal plans (Brenier's theorem) and closed formulas in dimension 1 and for Gaussians. This chapter derives the duality, then defines the Wasserstein distances and proves that they are distances.

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.1 — Kantorovich duality (complete proof in the discrete case)]{.tag}

::: key
[Key result — Kantorovich duality]{.tag}
$$
W_c(\mu, \nu) \;=\; \max_{(f, g) \in \Phi_c} \ \int f\, d\mu + \int g\, d\nu, \qquad \Phi_c = \big\{(f, g) \ :\ f(x) + g(y) \leq c(x, y)\ \forall (x,y)\big\}.
$$
:::

In the discrete case:
$$
\max_{f,g} \langle a, f\rangle + \langle b, g\rangle \quad \text{s.t.} \quad f_i + g_j \leq C_{ij}.
$$

::: proof
**Step 1 (the discrete problem is an LP).** The constraints $\Gamma \geq 0$, $\Gamma\mathbf{1} = a$, $\Gamma^\top\mathbf{1} = b$ are affine; the primal is feasible (e.g. $\Gamma = ab^\top$) and bounded ($\langle C,\Gamma\rangle \geq 0$).

**Step 2 (the dual).** Write the dual of th. 0.1 by associating a multiplier $f_i$ with the row constraint $\sum_j \Gamma_{ij} = a_i$ and $g_j$ with the column constraint $\sum_i \Gamma_{ij} = b_j$. The dual of $\min_{\Gamma \geq 0}\{\langle C, \Gamma\rangle\}$ under these equalities is
$$
\max_{f,g}\{\langle a, f\rangle + \langle b, g\rangle\ :\ f_i + g_j \leq C_{ij}\ \forall i,j\} .
$$
Each variable $\Gamma_{ij} \geq 0$ yields one dual inequality constraint.

**Step 3 (strong duality).** The primal is feasible and bounded ⇒ strong duality (th. 0.1): the optima exist and coincide.

**Step 4 (reading the complementarity).** At the optimal triple $(\Gamma^\star, f^\star, g^\star)$:
$$
\Gamma^\star_{ij} > 0 \ \Longrightarrow\ f^\star_i + g^\star_j = C_{ij},
$$
i.e. *mass travels only on saturated routes* — it is this condition that ties the plan to the potentials (corollary 2.3).[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: def
[Definition 2.2 — c-transform and Kantorovich potentials]{.tag} For a potential $f$, the c-transform is
$$
f^c(y) = \inf_x\, \big[c(x,y) - f(x)\big] .
$$
A potential $f$ is *c-concave* if $f = (f^c)^{\bar c}$ (bitransform).

At the optima of theorem 2.1, one may always assume $g^\star = (f^\star)^c$ and $f^\star = (g^\star)^{\bar c}$: replacing $g$ by $f^c \geq g$ can only *increase* the dual objective while remaining admissible. The optimal pair then reduces to **one** c-concave potential $f^\star$ (and its dual).
:::

::: cor
[Corollary 2.3 — Brenier's theorem (precise statement) and the quadratic case]{.tag} If $\mu \ll \mathrm{Leb}$ and $c(x,y) = \tfrac12\|x-y\|^2$:

-   the optimal plan is **unique** and induced by a map: $\gamma^\star = (\mathrm{Id}, T)_\#\mu$;
-   $T = \nabla\varphi$, the gradient of a convex function $\varphi$; conversely, every admissible map of this form is optimal (cyclical monotonicity);
-   link with the dual: $\varphi(x) = \tfrac12\|x\|^2 - f^\star(x)$, i.e. $\ T(x) = x - \nabla f^\star(x)$ on the transported support.

*Reading*: optimal transport is a **gradient** — it deforms space continuously, without tearing; in 1D, $T = F_\nu^{-1} \circ F_\mu$ (monotone rearrangement, prop. 2.6). For two Gaussians, $T$ is affine (th. 2.7).

In ML: $T$ = the "mapping" we learn to adapt a domain (ch. 4) — cf. the Deep Learning module for the networks that approximate it.
:::

::: def
[Definition 2.4 — Wasserstein distance of order $p$]{.tag} With $c = d^p$ on a metric space $(E, d)$: $$W_p(\mu, \nu) = \Big( \min_{\gamma \in \Pi(\mu,\nu)} \int d(x,y)^p\, d\gamma \Big)^{1/p}$$ on the set of probabilities with finite moment of order $p$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.5 — $W_p$ is a distance (proved: separation and triangle inequality by gluing)]{.tag}

::: proof
*Symmetry*: if $\gamma$ is admissible for $(\mu,\nu)$, its transpose is admissible for $(\nu,\mu)$, at the same cost.

*Separation*: $W_p(\mu,\nu) = 0$ ⇒ there exists an optimal $\gamma^\star$ with zero cost, supported on $\{x = y\}$ (since $d^p > 0$ off the diagonal); its marginals are then equal: $\mu = \nu$.

*Triangle inequality* (discrete): let $\gamma^{12}$ be optimal between $\mu^1, \mu^2$ and $\gamma^{23}$ optimal between $\mu^2, \mu^3$.

**Gluing.** Set
$$
\pi_{i\ell} \;=\; \sum_j\ \frac{\gamma^{12}_{ij}\,\gamma^{23}_{j\ell}}{\mu^2_j},
$$
the law of the pair $(X, Z)$ where we first draw $Y \sim \mu^2$, then $X \sim \gamma^{12}(\cdot\mid Y)$ and $Z \sim \gamma^{23}(Y, \cdot)$.

Marginals:
$$
\sum_\ell \pi_{i\ell} = \sum_j \gamma^{12}_{ij}\frac{\sum_\ell\gamma^{23}_{j\ell}}{\mu^2_j} = \sum_j \gamma^{12}_{ij} = \mu^1_i ,
$$
and likewise $\sum_i \pi_{i\ell} = \mu^3_\ell$. So $\pi$ is admissible for $(\mu^1, \mu^3)$.

We conclude by *conditional* Minkowski: the inequality
$$
\big(\mathbb{E}[d(X,Z)^p]\big)^{1/p} \leq \big(\mathbb{E}[d(X,Y)^p]\big)^{1/p} + \big(\mathbb{E}[d(Y,Z)^p]\big)^{1/p}
$$
is proved by applying Minkowski conditionally on $Y$, then integrating. Hence
$$
W_p(\mu^1,\mu^3) \leq \Big(\sum_{i\ell} \pi_{i\ell}\, d(x_i, z_\ell)^p\Big)^{1/p} \leq W_p(\mu^1,\mu^2) + W_p(\mu^2,\mu^3).
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[Narrow topology: what $W_p$ "sees"]{.tag} On probabilities with finite moment of order $p$, $W_p(\mu_k, \mu) \to 0$ ⇔ *narrow* convergence (against every bounded continuous test function) *+* convergence of the moments of order $p$.

Comparison with the usual divergences: $\mathrm{KL}(\mu\|\nu) = \infty$ as soon as the supports move apart, whereas $W_p$ stays finite and *continuous* — two clouds shifted by $\varepsilon$ are at distance $\varepsilon$ (not "infinity").

It is this "flat" geometry (no support jump) that makes $W$ usable in ML: informative gradients, and an interpolation in the physical sense of displacement,
$$
\mu_t = ((1-t)\,\mathrm{Id} + tT)_\#\mu .
$$
:::

:::: thm
[Proposition 2.6 — $W_p$ in dimension 1: coupling of quantiles (proved in the discrete case)]{.tag} $$W_p(\mu, \nu) = \Big(\int_0^1 \big|F_\mu^{-1}(u) - F_\nu^{-1}(u)\big|^p\, du\Big)^{1/p},$$ where $F^{-1}(u) = \inf\{x \ : \ F(x) \geq u\}$ is the quantile. The optimal plan matches the $u$-quantile of $\mu$ with the $u$-quantile of $\nu$; computable by sorting in $\mathcal{O}(n\log n)$.

::: proof
Discrete case, $n$ equal masses.

**Step 1 (uncrossing).** Consider a plan putting mass on $(x_1, y_2)$ and $(x_2, y_1)$ with $x_1 \leq x_2$ and $y_1 \leq y_2$ ("crossed routes"); move this mass to $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(x_2, y_2)$. The marginals are preserved and the cost does not increase, since
$$
|x_1 - y_2|^p + |x_2 - y_1|^p \ \geq\ |x_1 - y_1|^p + |x_2 - y_2|^p.
$$
Indeed, set
$$
a = x_1 - y_1, \qquad b = x_2 - y_2, \qquad d = y_2 - y_1 \geq 0 .
$$
The right-hand side is $\varphi(a) + \varphi(b)$ and the left one $\varphi(a - d) + \varphi(b + d)$, with $\varphi(t) = |t|^p$ convex for $p \geq 1$.

The two numbers $a - d$ and $b + d$ have the same sum as $a$ and $b$, and they enclose them.

Indeed, $a - d \leq a \leq b + d$ because $x_1 \leq x_2$, and $a - d \leq b$ because $b - (a - d) = x_2 - x_1 \geq 0$.

Hence $a = \lambda (a - d) + (1-\lambda)(b + d)$ for some $\lambda \in [0, 1]$, and then $b = (1-\lambda)(a - d) + \lambda (b + d)$. By convexity we get a convex rearrangement inequality:
$$
\varphi(a) + \varphi(b) \leq \varphi(a - d) + \varphi(b + d) .
$$

**Step 2.** By iterating the uncrossing, an optimal plan exists that crosses no pair: it is the monotone coupling $x_i \leftrightarrow y_{\sigma(i)}$ with increasing $\sigma$ — the quantile matching.

**Step 3 (general case, statement).** For arbitrary laws, the plan $(F_\mu^{-1}(U), F_\nu^{-1}(U))$ with $U \sim \mathcal{U}[0,1]$ has the right marginals and is monotone, hence optimal (1D Brenier).[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.7 — $W_2$ between Gaussians: the Bures metric (proved)]{.tag} $$W_2^2\big(\mathcal{N}(m_1,\Sigma_1), \mathcal{N}(m_2,\Sigma_2)\big) = \|m_1 - m_2\|^2 + \mathrm{tr}\Big(\Sigma_1 + \Sigma_2 - 2\big(\Sigma_1^{1/2}\,\Sigma_2\,\Sigma_1^{1/2}\big)^{1/2}\Big).$$

::: proof
**Step 1 (centering).** For every coupling $(X, Y)$,
$$
\mathbb{E}\|X - Y\|^2 = \|m_1 - m_2\|^2 + \mathbb{E}\|\tilde X - \tilde Y\|^2
$$
with $\tilde X, \tilde Y$ centered (expand the square, the cross terms cancel). Means and covariances transport separately, and the plan $(m_1 + \tilde X,\ m_2 + \tilde Y)$ attains the bound. Assume $m_1 = m_2 = 0$.

**Step 2 (an affine candidate).** Set $M = \Sigma_1^{1/2}\Sigma_2\Sigma_1^{1/2}$ and
$$
A \;=\; \Sigma_1^{-1/2}\, M^{1/2}\, \Sigma_1^{-1/2}.
$$
$A$ is symmetric positive definite (a symmetric conjugate of $M^{1/2}$). The coupling $(X, Y = AX)$ with $X \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma_1)$ is admissible: $Y$ is a centered Gaussian with covariance
$$
A\Sigma_1A^\top = \Sigma_1^{-1/2}M\Sigma_1^{-1/2} = \Sigma_2 .
$$

**Step 3 (cost of the candidate).** We have
$$
\mathbb{E}\|X - AX\|^2 = \mathrm{tr}\big((I - A)\Sigma_1(I - A)^\top\big) = \mathrm{tr}(\Sigma_1) - 2\,\mathrm{tr}(A\Sigma_1) + \mathrm{tr}(\Sigma_2) .
$$
Now, by cyclicity,
$$
\mathrm{tr}(A\Sigma_1) = \mathrm{tr}\big(\Sigma_1^{-1/2}M^{1/2}\Sigma_1^{1/2}\big) = \mathrm{tr}\big(M^{1/2}\big),
$$
so the cost is
$$
\mathrm{tr}(\Sigma_1 + \Sigma_2) - 2\,\mathrm{tr}(M^{1/2}),
$$
the announced formula.

**Step 4 (optimality via Brenier).** $T(x) = Ax = \nabla\big(\tfrac12 x^\top A x\big)$ is the gradient of a convex function (A symmetric ≥ 0) that sends $\mu$ onto $\nu$; by the converse of corollary 2.3 (sufficiency of cyclical monotonicity), this coupling is *optimal*. In 1D, $A = \sigma_2/\sigma_1$: cost $(\sigma_1 - \sigma_2)^2$, consistent with prop. 2.6.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: cor
[Corollary 2.8 — Wasserstein barycenter of 1D Gaussians (proved)]{.tag} The barycenter of the laws $\mu_k = \mathcal{N}(m_k, \sigma_k^2)$ with weights $\sum w_k = 1$,
$$
\arg\min_\nu \sum_k w_k\, W_2^2(\nu, \mu_k),
$$
is the Gaussian
$$
\mathcal{N}\Big(\sum_k w_k m_k,\ \ \big(\sum_k w_k \sigma_k\big)^{2}\Big).
$$

::: proof
By prop. 2.6, minimizing over $\nu$ amounts to minimizing
$$
\sum_k w_k \int_0^1 |F_\nu^{-1}(u) - F_k^{-1}(u)|^2du
$$
in the quantile function $F_\nu^{-1}$.

Pointwise in $u$, the optimization is a simple regression: the optimum (zero derivative — strictly convex function) is
$$
F_\nu^{-1}(u) = \sum_k w_k F_k^{-1}(u) .
$$
Now $F_k^{-1}(u) = m_k + \sigma_k\,\Phi^{-1}(u)$, so
$$
F_\nu^{-1}(u) = \underbrace{\sum_k w_k m_k}_{m} + \underbrace{\sum_k w_k\sigma_k}_{\sigma}\,\Phi^{-1}(u),
$$
which is exactly the quantile of $\mathcal{N}(m, \sigma^2)$.

Note that the "barycenter variance" $\sigma^2 = (\sum w_k\sigma_k)^2$ is the square of the *mean of the standard deviations* — not the mean of the variances.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[Bridge with the Signal Processing module]{.tag} The Bures formula of theorem 2.7 is *exactly* the Fréchet distance (FID) used to evaluate image generators and audio models: cf. the Signal Processing module M1P1, chapter 8, which prepares this reading — and whose "spectral loss" is a Gaussian $W_2$ loss on spectrograms. The same mathematical object runs through both modules.
:::

## 3. Entropic regularization: Sinkhorn {#ch3}

Exact transport is a linear program whose cost grows like $n^3 \log n$ and whose solution is not differentiable in the data. Adding a small entropy term makes the problem strictly convex, solvable by a few matrix-vector products (the Sinkhorn algorithm) and smooth — the version of OT that machine learning actually uses.

::: def
[Definition 3.1 — Entropic OT (Cuturi, 2013)]{.tag}
$$
W_\varepsilon(a, b) \;=\; \min_{\Gamma \in U(a, b)}\ \langle C, \Gamma\rangle + \varepsilon\, \mathrm{KL}\big(\Gamma\,\big\|\, a b^\top\big),
$$
where $U(a,b)$ is the polytope of marginals. The problem is strictly convex (the entropy is, prop. 0.3) ⇒ **unique solution**, which converges to a solution of the LP as $\varepsilon \to 0$.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.2 — Form of the minimizer and the Sinkhorn algorithm (proved)]{.tag} The unique solution reads
$$
\Gamma^\varepsilon = \mathrm{diag}(u)\, K\, \mathrm{diag}(v), \qquad K = e^{-C/\varepsilon},
$$
and the scaling vectors are obtained by the alternating iterations

::: key
[Key result — Sinkhorn iterations]{.tag}
$$
u \leftarrow a\,/\,(K v), \qquad v \leftarrow b\,/\,(K^\top u).
$$
:::

::: proof
**Form (optimality conditions).** Lagrangian with multipliers $\lambda_i$ (rows) and $\mu_j$ (columns):
$$
\mathcal{L} = \langle C,\Gamma\rangle + \varepsilon\sum_{ij}\Gamma_{ij} \log\frac{\Gamma_{ij}}{a_ib_j} - \lambda^\top(\Gamma\mathbf{1} - a) - \mu^\top(\Gamma^\top\mathbf{1} - b) .
$$
At $\Gamma^\star$, for each $(i,j)$:
$$
C_{ij} + \varepsilon\Big(\log\frac{\Gamma_{ij}}{a_ib_j} + 1\Big) - \lambda_i - \mu_j - \varepsilon = 0 \ \Rightarrow\ \Gamma^\star_{ij} = a_i b_j\, e^{(\lambda_i + \mu_j - C_{ij})/\varepsilon} = u_i K_{ij} v_j,
$$
with $u_i = a_i\, e^{\lambda_i/\varepsilon}$ and $v_j = b_j\, e^{\mu_j/\varepsilon}$ (the weights $a_i, b_j$ are absorbed into the scaling vectors).

**Iterations (Bregman projections).** The constraints $\Gamma\mathbf{1} = a$ and $\Gamma^\top\mathbf{1} = b$ are not separated: we alternately project $K$ onto each constraint in the sense of the Bregman divergence $\mathrm{KL}(\cdot\|\cdot)$.

Consider the projection of $\tilde\Gamma = \mathrm{diag}(u)K\, \mathrm{diag}(v)$ onto $\{\Gamma\mathbf{1} = a\}$, i.e. the minimization of $\mathrm{KL}(\Gamma\|\tilde\Gamma)$ under the row constraint. Setting to zero the derivative
$$
\partial/\partial\Gamma_{ij}\big[\sum\Gamma_{ij}\log(\Gamma_{ij}/\tilde\Gamma_{ij}) - \rho_i(\sum_j\Gamma_{ij} - a_i)\big] = \log(\Gamma_{ij}/\tilde\Gamma_{ij}) + 1 - \rho_i
$$
gives $\Gamma_{ij} = e^{\rho_i - 1}\tilde\Gamma_{ij}$: a *rescaling of the rows*, exactly $u \leftarrow a/(Kv)$; likewise for the columns.

Each iteration divides the violation of the other constraint; the sequence converges to the point with the prescribed marginals — the unique point of the polytope of the form $\mathrm{diag}(u)K\,\mathrm{diag}(v)$.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: thm
[Theorem 3.3 — Geometric convergence (Franklin & Lorenz, 1989)]{.tag} For $K > 0$ (finite costs, $\varepsilon > 0$), Sinkhorn converges at a **geometric** rate. The scaling vectors converge in Hilbert's projective metric, which each half-iteration contracts by the factor $\tanh(\Delta/4)$, where
$$
\Delta = \max_{i,j,k,l} \log\frac{K_{ik}K_{jl}}{K_{jk}K_{il}}
$$
measures the spread of the coefficients of $K$.

Since $\Delta \leq 2\max_{ij} C_{ij}/\varepsilon$, convergence is all the faster as $\varepsilon$ is large. In practice: 20 to 200 iterations for 3-digit accuracy (at moderate $\varepsilon$).
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 3.4 — Gradient of the regularized loss (sketch: envelope/implicit differentiation)]{.tag} $$\nabla_a\, W_\varepsilon(a, b) = f^\star \quad (\text{optimal dual potential}).$$

::: proof
The Lagrangian of the problem (that of th. 3.2) has a saddle point at $(\Gamma^\star, \lambda^\star, \mu^\star)$, at which
$$
W_\varepsilon(a,b) = \mathcal{L}(\Gamma^\star,\lambda^\star,\mu^\star).
$$

Differentiate with respect to $a$. Since the Lagrangian is stationary in $\Gamma$ and in the multipliers at the saddle point, their variations contribute nothing, and only the explicit dependence on $a$ remains — the term $\lambda^\top a$, and the term $-\varepsilon\sum_{ij}\Gamma_{ij}\log a_i$ of the entropy, whose derivative is
$$
-\varepsilon\sum_j \Gamma^\star_{ij}/a_i = -\varepsilon .
$$
Hence
$$
\partial W_\varepsilon/\partial a_i = \lambda^\star_i - \varepsilon .
$$
The gradient is the optimal dual potential, up to an additive constant that is irrelevant on the simplex ($\sum_i a_i = 1$). This is the envelope theorem — *only the multiplier matters*, the plan itself contributes nothing.

Practical consequence: a loss $a = a_\theta$ (a batch of features, parameters $\theta$) can be differentiated without re-differentiating the Sinkhorn iterations: we backpropagate the **potential**, not the plan.[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
["Debiased" Sinkhorn divergences and epsilon-scaling]{.tag}

-   **Entropic bias**: $W_\varepsilon(a,a) > 0$ (the regularized plan "blurs" even between identical distributions) and the plan is concentrated near $ab^\top$ as $\varepsilon \to \infty$. Correction (Feydy et al., AISTATS 2019): $$S_\varepsilon(a,b) = W_\varepsilon(a,b) - \tfrac12 W_\varepsilon(a,a) - \tfrac12 W_\varepsilon(b,b) \ \geq\ 0, \qquad S_\varepsilon(a,a) = 0,$$ which interpolates between $W$ (ε→0) and a kernel distance (MMD, ε→∞) — the loss of choice for comparing clouds in deep learning.
-   **ε-scaling**: at small $\varepsilon$, $K = e^{-C/\varepsilon}$ is numerically degenerate (its smallest entries underflow): start at large $\varepsilon$ (fast convergence), then divide it by \~2 down to the target, reusing $(u, v)$ warm; stabilized variants in log space (`ot.sinkhorn_log`).
-   **GPU and complexity**: one iteration = two matrix-vector products ($\mathcal{O}(n^2)$), fully parallelizable and "batchable" (thousands of problems at once on GPU); the exact LP ($\mathcal{O}(n^3 \log n)$) lacks this memory regularity — hence Sinkhorn's supremacy in high dimension.
:::

::: def
[Definition 3.5 — Sliced transport (1D projections)]{.tag}
$$
\mathrm{SW}_p^p(\mu,\nu) = \int_{\mathbb{S}^{d-1}} W_p^p\big(\theta_\#\mu,\ \theta_\#\nu\big)\,d\theta,
$$
the average of the 1D $W_p$ of the projections onto all directions $\theta$. It is computable by sorting (prop. 2.6) and estimated by Monte-Carlo over $L$ directions: $\mathcal{O}(L\,n\log n)$, with *no* $n \times n$ cost matrix.

Statistical benefits: no curse of dimensionality (estimating $\mathrm{SW}$ converges at $n^{-1/2}$, versus $n^{-1/d}$ for $W_p$) — see Tanguy, Flamary & Delon (2024) for the fine analysis of empirical projections. It is also the natural language for the spectrograms of the Signal Processing module (ch. 9): projecting = marginalizing.
:::

```python
import numpy as np
import ot                              # POT: Python Optimal Transport

n = 200
xs, xt = np.random.RandomState(0).normal(0, 1, (n, 2)), np.random.RandomState(1).normal([2, 0], [0.5, 2], (n, 2))
a, b = np.ones(n) / n, np.ones(n) / n
C = ot.dist(xs, xt)                    # squared costs ||x-y||^2

G = ot.emd(a, b, C)                    # exact OT (LP, transport simplex)
G0 = ot.emd2(a, b, C)                  # value only (exact W2^2)
Gs = ot.sinkhorn(a, b, C / C.max(), reg=0.05)
print("exact  :", (G * C).sum())
print("sinkhorn:", (Gs * C).sum())     # slight entropy overhead
print("sliced  :", ot.sliced_wasserstein_distance(xs, xt, n_projections=500))

# 1D: quantiles (prop. 2.6) -- exact W2 computed by sorting
print("W2 1d :", ot.wasserstein_1d(xs[:,0], xt[:,0], p=2)**0.5)
```

## 4. OT and machine learning {#ch4}

With the tools of ch. 1–3 in hand, this chapter uses transport to solve learning problems: adapting a classifier to a shifted domain, training generative models with a Wasserstein loss, averaging distributions, comparing documents — and asks how many samples are needed to estimate a Wasserstein distance.

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Domain adaptation, covariate shift]{.tag} A **domain adaptation** problem provides a labeled *source* $(x_i, y_i)_{i \leq n} \sim \mu_S$ on $\mathcal{X} \times \mathcal{Y}$ and an unlabeled *target* $(z_j)_{j \leq m} \sim \mu_T$ on $\mathcal{X}$.

Working assumption (*covariate shift*): the labeling rule $P(Y \mid X)$ is the same in both domains, but the marginals $\mu_S \neq \mu_T$ (sensors, populations, image styles…).

A classifier trained on the source suffers from the distribution shift; the OT idea: **transport the source onto the target** before learning — exactly Monge's problem of ch. 1, applied to clouds of features.
:::

::: thm
[OTDA algorithm — transport, propagate the labels, predict (Courty, Flamary et al., IEEE TPAMI 2016)]{.tag}

1.  **Costs**: $C_{ij} = \|x_i - z_j\|^2$ (centered-scaled features, possibly kernel or deep features, cf. the Deep Learning module M1P1, chapter 7 "transfer learning").
2.  **Class regularization**: we additionally know that the $x_i$ carry labels — we penalize plans that scatter a single class, via a convex group-lasso-type penalty on the rows of $\Gamma$ (the points of a same class are transported *to the same place*). Final cost: $\langle C, \Gamma\rangle$ + class penalty, solved by LP (ch. 1) or by regularized Sinkhorn (ch. 3).
3.  **Barycentric transport**: each source point is sent to the plan-weighted average of its images: $$\hat T(x_i) \;=\; \frac{1}{a_i}\sum_j\ \Gamma_{ij}\, z_j,$$ and its label $y_i$ follows (the plan is a *soft coupling*, not a map: this is the Monge barycentric map, optimal for $c = \|\cdot\|^2$ by corollary 2.3). **Label propagation** follows: the label predicted for $z_j$ is the (plan-weighted) majority of the classes arriving at $z_j$.
4.  **Learning**: train the classifier on the transported pairs $(\hat T(x_i),\, y_i)$ — which live in the *target* space — then predict on the target.
5.  **Out-of-sample**: a new point $z$ is predicted directly (it is already in the target space); to transport a new *source* point without recomputing the plan, interpolate the plan row of the $k$ nearest neighbors of $x$ in the source, or learn a map $T_\theta \approx \hat T$ (a network, Deep Learning module).

*Positioning*: the module's instructor is a co-author of the paper — detailed in ch. 7.

The **JDOT** extension (Courty, Flamary et al., NeurIPS 2017) transports the *joint* law $(X, Y)$ with a cost that includes the label loss,
$$
c\big((x,y),(z,y')\big) = \alpha\|x - z\|^2 + \mathcal{L}(y, y'),
$$
which gives unsupervised *and* semi-supervised adaptation in the same framework.
:::

:::: thm
[Proposition 4.2 — Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality, or why GANs are called "Wasserstein" (proved sketch)]{.tag} For $c = d$ (a distance), $$W_1(\mu, \nu) \;=\; \sup_{\|f\|_{\mathrm{Lip}} \leq 1}\ \int f\, d\mu - \int f\, d\nu,$$ the sup being taken over the **1-Lipschitz** functions.

::: proof
Start from the duality of th. 2.1 with $c = d$ and replace $g$ by the c-transform $g = f^c$ (def. 2.2: this does not decrease the objective). For a distance cost,
$$
f^c(y) = \inf_x\,[\,d(x,y) - f(x)\,] .
$$

If $f$ is 1-Lipschitz, taking $x = y$ gives $f^c(y) = -f(y)$, because the infimum is attained at $x = y$: indeed $f(x) \leq f(y) + d(x,y)$, i.e.
$$
d(x,y) - f(x) \geq -f(y) .
$$
The dual then equals $\int f\,d\mu - \int f\, d\nu$.

Conversely, the constraint $f(x) + f^c(y) \leq d(x,y)$ with $y \to x$ forces $|f(x) - f(x')| \leq d(x, x')$: every admissible dual pair can be written (up to normalization) with a 1-Lipschitz $f$ — hence the formula (complete proof: Villani 2009, th. 5.10).[∎]{.qed}
:::

The **WGAN** (Arjovsky, Chintala & Bottou, ICML 2017) minimizes precisely this quantity between the law of the data and that of a generator $G_\theta$:
$$
\min_\theta\ \max_{D_\phi\ \mathrm{1\!-\!Lip}}\ \mathbb{E}_{x \sim \mathrm{data}}[D_\phi(x)] \ -\ \mathbb{E}_{z \sim p(z)}[D_\phi(G_\theta(z))],
$$
the "critic" $D_\phi$ playing the role of a parametrized Kantorovich potential (the dual of th. 2.1 makes the loss *differentiable in $\theta$*).

The 1-Lipschitz constraint in practice: weight clipping, gradient penalty (Gulrajani et al., 2017), spectral normalization (Miyato et al., 2018) — cf. the Deep Learning module M1P1, chapter 9 (generative models). A modern computable alternative: the debiased Sinkhorn loss of ch. 3 (th. 3.4: we backpropagate the potential), available with PyTorch/JAX backends in POT.
::::

::: def
[Definition 4.3 — Wasserstein barycenter (Agueh & Carlier, 2011)]{.tag} For measures $\mu_1, \dots, \mu_K$ and weights $w \in \Delta_K$ (the *simplex*): $$\mathrm{Bar}(\mu_1, \dots, \mu_K; w) \;=\; \arg\min_{\nu}\ \sum_{k=1}^{K} w_k\, W_2^2(\nu, \mu_k).$$ The 1D Gaussian case is solved explicitly by corollary 2.8 (barycentric quantiles). General cases:

-   **Fixed support** (a grid of $p$ points): the problem is convex in the barycenter weights — quadratic programming (Agueh-Carlier) or *iterative* Sinkhorn;
-   **Iterated Bregman projections (IBP)**: the entropic version (Benamou et al., 2015): initialize $\Gamma_k$ independently for each $k$, then repeat for each $k$ a Sinkhorn scaling step (th. 3.2) toward the common barycenter mass, then a rescaling toward the marginal $\mu_k$ — a "squared" Sinkhorn iteration, parallelizable;
-   **Free support** (Cuturi & Doucet, 2014): optimize *positions and weights* of the barycenter points by alternating: (i) plans $\Gamma_k$ toward each measure (OT), (ii) moving the barycenter points toward the barycenter of their images — the multi-measure extension of the barycentric transport formula of the OTDA algorithm.

Applications: interpolation of shapes and distributions, color transfer (histograms), atlases and averages in medical imaging, signal normalization (ch. 7: Convolutional Monge Mapping), barycenters of graphs (ch. 5, FGW). POT: `ot.bregman.barycenter`, `ot.lp.free_support_barycenter`.
:::

::: ex
[Example 4.4 — Word Mover's Distance: the distance between documents as OT (Kusner et al., ICML 2015)]{.tag} A document is a **distribution over the embeddings of its words**: $a_i \propto$ frequency (or frequency × idf) of word $i$, point $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^d$ its embedding (word2vec/GloVe — cf. the Text Mining and NLP module M1P2, chapter 4).

The **WMD** between two documents is simply $W_1$ between these two discrete distributions, with the Euclidean cost between embeddings: the transport plan "explains" the semantic proximity: "Obama" speaks to "president", "France" to "Germany".

For large-scale nearest-neighbor search, lower bounds (relaxed distances between centroids) are precomputed so that exact OT is solved only on the candidates.

```python
import numpy as np, ot
# two partially shared "documents", fictitious embeddings
X = np.array([[0., 0.], [1., 0.], [10., 0.]])     # king, queen, cat (source)
Y = np.array([[0.1, 0.], [1.2, 0.], [10.4, 0.]])  # queen, king, dog  (target)
a = np.array([.5, .3, .2]); b = np.array([.4, .4, .2])
C = ot.dist(X, Y, metric="euclidean")              # Euclidean costs (WMD is a W_1)
print("WMD :", ot.emd2(a, b, C))                   # exact plan: ot.emd(a, b, C)
```
:::

::: note
[Spectral loss: Gaussian $W_2$ as a closed-form, differentiable loss]{.tag} Compare two *batches* of generative data (images, audio) by fitting a Gaussian to their features and evaluating $W_2^2$ with the closed formula of theorem 2.7 (Bures metric): this is the FID of image generators and the "Fréchet audio distance" of audio generators — a loss *without a solver*, differentiable, usable as a training loss (spectral loss).

This is exactly the announced bridge with the Signal Processing module M1P1: chapter 8 (FID and Bures are presented there) and chapter 9 (bridge lab). In 1D (spectra, signals), return to quantiles (prop. 2.6); `ot.gaussian.wass2` provides the Gaussian empirical estimate.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 4.5 — Statistical estimation of $W$: the curse of dimensionality, and the Sinkhorn exception (statement)]{.tag} Let $\mu_n$ be the empirical measure of $n$ i.i.d. points $\sim \mu$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$. Then:

-   **Exact OT**: $\mathbb{E}\,W_p(\mu_n, \mu) \asymp n^{-1/d}$ for $d > 2p$ (Dudley; sharp bounds by Fournier & Guillin, 2015). In high dimension, the empirical $W_p$ distance between *two samples of the same law* remains of constant order — the "noise" does not decrease: using exact $W_p$ as a loss in high dimension is statistically fragile;
-   **Debiased Sinkhorn**: the divergence $S_\varepsilon$ of ch. 3 (debiased) is estimated at the **parametric rate $n^{-1/2}$** under regularity assumptions (Genevay, Chizat, Bach, Peyré & Rigollet, AISTATS 2019); the same holds for the sliced distance (def. 3.5, 1D projections).

| Comparator | Empirical rate | Cost for $n$ points | Differentiable? |
|---|---|---|---|
| exact $W_p$ | $n^{-1/d}$ | $\mathcal{O}(n^3 \log n)$ | subgradients only |
| Sinkhorn $W_\varepsilon$, $S_\varepsilon$ | $n^{-1/2}$ (debiased) | $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ / iteration | yes (potential, th. 3.4) |
| sliced $\mathrm{SW}_p$ | $n^{-1/2}$ | $\mathcal{O}(L\, n\log n)$ | yes (sorting) |
| Gaussian $W_2$ (Bures) | parametric (if Gaussian) | $\mathcal{O}(d^3)$ | yes (closed form) |

*Reading*: in small dimension or in 1D, exact OT (quantiles); in high dimension, regularize (entropy, projections, Gaussian). This is the rule applied in all the labs of this module.
:::

## 5. Gromov-Wasserstein and beyond {#ch5}

Sometimes the two distributions live in different spaces — two graphs with unrelated node sets, two word-embedding spaces of different languages — so that no cost $c(x, y)$ between their points exists. Gromov-Wasserstein compares instead the *internal* distances of each space; this chapter defines it, proves its invariance, and gives its algorithms and its variants for attributed graphs and data matrices.

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — Gromov-Wasserstein transport (Mémoli, 2011)]{.tag} The two clouds live in *incomparable* spaces: we have no cross cost $c(x, y)$, only *internal* structures — distance matrices $D \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ (source) and $D' \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times m}$ (target). The quadratic problem:
$$
\mathrm{GW}_2^2(D, D'; a, b) \;=\; \min_{\Gamma \in U(a,b)}\ \sum_{i,k,j,l} \big(D_{ik} - D'_{jl}\big)^2\ \Gamma_{ij}\,\Gamma_{kl},
$$
that is,
$$
\min_\gamma \mathbb{E}\big[\,\big(\mathcal{D}(X, X') - \mathcal{D}'(Y, Y')\big)^2\,\big]
$$
where $(X, Y)$ and $(X', Y')$ are i.i.d. with law $\gamma$: we look for the coupling that makes the **pairs of internal distances as equal as possible**.

Interpretation: preserve the neighborhoods, the triangles, the "shape" — not the positions. The problem is *non-convex* in $\Gamma$ (quadratic): local minima, important initialization — a complete contrast with ch. 1.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.2 — Isometric invariance of GW (proved as a sketch)]{.tag} Let $\varphi$ be an **isometry** between the structured spaces, with $\varphi_\#\mu = \nu$:
$$
\mathcal{D}'(\varphi(x), \varphi(x')) = \mathcal{D}(x, x') \quad \text{for all } x, x'.
$$
Then
$$
\mathrm{GW}_2(\mu, \nu) = 0 .
$$
Conversely (Mémoli): $\mathrm{GW}_2(\mu, \nu) = 0$ if and only if such a measure-preserving isometry exists.

::: proof
The diagonal plan $\gamma^\star = (\mathrm{Id}, \varphi)_\#\mu$ is admissible (marginals $\mu$ and $\varphi_\#\mu = \nu$). For two copies $(X, \varphi(X))$ and $(X', \varphi(X'))$ i.i.d. from $\gamma^\star$, each term of the quadratic sum vanishes *pointwise*, by the definition of an isometry:
$$
\big(\mathcal{D}(X, X') - \mathcal{D}'(\varphi(X), \varphi(X'))\big)^2 = 0 .
$$
The cost is 0, and 0 is the lower bound (a sum of squares).

The converse: a zero cost forces $\mathcal{D}(X, X') = \mathcal{D}'(Y, Y')$ $\gamma$-almost surely; the support of $\gamma^\star$ (compact, closed) then defines the sought isometry between the supports (a closure argument, admitted).[∎]{.qed}
:::

Practical consequence: GW is **invariant under rotations, translations, reflections, changes of frame** — where $W_2$ "sees" the absolute offset of the clouds (and equals $\|\text{translation}\|$ even for two isometric copies). It is the right distance for aligning objects defined up to an isometry: graphs, proteins, surfaces, heterogeneous embedding spaces.
::::

::: thm
[GW algorithms: projected (PGW), entropic, sliced (SGW)]{.tag}

-   **Projected GW — PGW** (Peyré, Cuturi & Solomon, ICML 2016): linearize the quadratic problem around the current plan $\Gamma^{(t)}$. The gradient of the objective in $\Gamma$ reads
    $$
    c^{(t)}_{ij} \;=\; \sum_{k,l}\ \big(D_{ik} - D'_{jl}\big)^2\ \Gamma^{(t)}_{kl} \;=\; \big[(D \odot D)\,a\big]_i + \big[(D' \odot D')\,b\big]_j - 2\,\big[D\,\Gamma^{(t)}\,D'^\top\big]_{ij},
    $$
    using $\Gamma^{(t)}\mathbf{1} = a$ and $\Gamma^{(t)\top}\mathbf{1} = b$, where $\odot$ is the entrywise product (in matrix form: two matrix-matrix products, $\mathcal{O}(n^2 m)$).

    We then iterate: *solve the linear OT with cost $c^{(t)}$* (exact LP or Sinkhorn) → new plan $\Gamma^{(t+1)}$. This is a conditional-gradient (Frank-Wolfe) scheme: with a line search between $\Gamma^{(t)}$ and the new plan, the GW value decreases at each iteration and the iterates reach a stationary point — in practice a *local minimum*, hence the importance of the initialization.
-   **Entropic GW** (Solomon, Peyré, Kim & Sra, SIGGRAPH 2016): regularize each linearized subproblem by $\varepsilon\,\mathrm{KL}$ and solve it by Sinkhorn (ch. 3): dense and smooth plans, GPU, but entropic blur — ε-scaling is used. In POT this is `ot.gromov.entropic_gromov_wasserstein` (parameter `epsilon`); `ot.gromov.gromov_wasserstein` is the unregularized conditional-gradient solver.
-   **SGW** (Vayer et al., NeurIPS 2019): project the structures onto 1D lines and average — the sliced analogue of ch. 3, speeds of $\mathcal{O}(L n\log n)$ and no statistical curse.
:::

::: def
[Definition 5.3 — Fused Gromov-Wasserstein: features *and* structure (Vayer, Chapel, Flamary, Tavenard & Courty, ICML 2019)]{.tag} When the objects *also* carry comparable attributes (features $F \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$, $F' \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times d'}$ with a cross cost $C_F(x_i, y_j)$, typically $\|F_i - F'_j\|^2$ after aligning the dimensions):
$$
\mathrm{FGW}_{\alpha} \;=\; \min_{\Gamma \in U(a,b)}\ (1-\alpha)\sum_{i,k,j,l} \big(D_{ik} - D'_{jl}\big)^2 \Gamma_{ij}\Gamma_{kl} \;+\; \alpha \sum_{i,j} C_F(x_i, y_j)\,\Gamma_{ij}.
$$

The parameter **$\alpha \in [0, 1]$** arbitrates between fidelity to the *attributes* ($\alpha = 1$: pure Wasserstein on the features) and fidelity to the **structure** ($\alpha = 0$: pure GW). The paper shows a form of continuity of the distance in $\alpha$ and bounds between FGW and its two extremes. The algorithm: PGW applied to the combined cost (the same linearization iteration).

This is *the* distance for **attributed graphs**: molecules (atoms: features; bonds: structure), social networks, brains — cf. the Graph ML module M1P2, chapter 5 (GNNs: message passing combines exactly attributes and structure) and chapter 9 (graph generation/evaluation). The FGW barycenter of several graphs defines a graph "average" (Vayer et al.).
:::

::: def
[Definition 5.4 — COOT: co-optimal transport over rows and columns (Redko, Vayer, Flamary & Courty, NeurIPS 2020)]{.tag} Two *data matrices* $X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$ (objects as rows, variables as columns) and $Y \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times p}$ — object *and* variable dimensions possibly different. COOT looks for **two couplings**, $\pi \in U(a, c)$ between the rows and $\sigma \in U(b, d)$ between the columns:
$$
\min_{\pi, \sigma}\ \sum_{i,j,k,l}\ \big(X_{ik} - Y_{jl}\big)^2\ \pi_{ij}\, \sigma_{kl},
$$
solved by **alternation**: with $\sigma$ fixed, the problem in $\pi$ is a linear OT with cost $\sum_{kl}(X_{ik} - Y_{jl})^2\sigma_{kl}$ (and symmetrically).

COOT unifies and generalizes: classical OT (a single cross-cost matrix), GW (when $X$ and $Y$ are themselves internal distance matrices $D, D'$), co-clustering and **heterogeneous domain adaptation** (aligning simultaneously samples *and* sensors/features — for example two EEG datasets with different electrodes). Here again: non-convex alternation, local minimum, initialization by OT or k-means.
:::

::: ex
[Example 5.5 — Alignment of graphs and knowledge graphs (an LLGA application), in POT]{.tag} Align two graphs (nodes with no given correspondence): GW on the adjacency/distance matrices; if the nodes carry attributes, FGW. Typical use cases in the master's program:

-   alignment of **knowledge graphs** (entities/relations of two bases, cf. the Graph ML module, chapter 10 on GraphRAG: disambiguating the common entities);
-   alignment of two word embedding spaces *without a dictionary* — Gromov-Wasserstein alignment of word embedding spaces (Alvarez-Melis & Jaakkola, EMNLP 2018): GW between the internal similarity matrices of two languages aligns the spaces in an unsupervised way (the plan connects words with the same neighborhoods) — a direct link with the Text Mining and NLP module, chapter 4.

```python
import numpy as np, ot                          # POT: ot.gromov

# two graphs: adjacencies (structure) + node attributes
A1 = np.array([[0., 1., 1.], [1., 0., 0.], [1., 0., 0.]])   # star
A2 = np.array([[0., 1., 0.], [1., 0., 1.], [0., 1., 0.]])   # path
D1 = 1.0 - A1                                   # short distances = edges
D2 = 1.0 - A2
a = np.ones(3) / 3 ; b = np.ones(3) / 3

# exact GW (PGW without regularization): node alignment plan
G = ot.gromov.gromov_wasserstein(D1, D2, a, b, loss_fun='square_loss')
print("GW2^2 :", ot.gromov.gromov_wasserstein2(D1, D2, a, b))

# FGW: add node attributes (same dimension here)
F1 = np.array([[0., 0.], [1., 0.], [0., 1.]])
F2 = np.array([[0.1, 0.], [0.9, 0.1], [0.2, 0.8]])
Cf = ot.dist(F1, F2)
Gf, log = ot.gromov.fused_gromov_wasserstein(Cf, D1, D2, a, b,
                                             loss_fun='square_loss', alpha=0.5,
                                             log=True)
print("FGW(a=0.5) :", log['fgw_dist'])
```

Lab remark: test several initializations (GW is non-convex), plot the distance as a function of $\alpha$ (FGW continuity), compare with the known exact alignment (synthetic sets of isomorphic graphs: GW = 0, th. 5.2).
:::

::: note
[The CMAP/POT GW bestiary]{.tag} The ecosystem developed around the instructor: semi-relaxed GW (only one side preserved — ICLR 2022), *unbalanced* fused GW for brain alignment (fugw, NeurIPS 2022), sliced GW, graph barycenters for prediction (NeurIPS 2022), and the complete integration into POT (`ot.gromov`: `gromov_wasserstein`, `fused_gromov_wasserstein`, `co_optimal_transport`…). Positioning with respect to the course: ch. 5 lays the definitions; these variants each fix a practical limitation (unequal masses, size, attributes) — details in ch. 7.
:::

## 6. Fairness through transport {#ch6}

A model trained on historical data reproduces the disparities between groups that these data contain. Fairness criteria compare the *distributions* of decisions across groups, so transport — which moves one distribution onto another at minimal cost — gives a natural way to repair the data or the decisions while changing them as little as possible.

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — The framework: sensitive attribute, demographic parity, equalized odds]{.tag} Data $(X, S, Y)$: features, **sensitive attribute** $S$ (gender, origin…), label $Y$; predictor $\hat Y = h(X)$ (possibly randomized). Two emblematic criteria:

-   **Demographic parity** (DP): $\hat Y$ independent of $S$ — the same positive decision rates per group;
-   **Equalized odds** (EO, Hardt, Price & Srebro, 2016): $\hat Y$ independent of $S$ *given* $Y$ — the same true positive *and* false positive rates per group.

OT enters both scenarios: (i) *pre-processing* — repair the feature distribution with a Wasserstein barycenter; (ii) *post-processing* — couple the per-group score distributions. In both cases, the central object is a **coupling**, i.e. a transport plan as in ch. 1.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.2 — Repair by Wasserstein barycenter (Gordaliza, Del Barrio, Gamboa & Loubes, ICML 2019)]{.tag} **Algorithm (full repair, scalar case then multivariate).**

1.  Estimate the conditional laws $\mu_s = \mathcal{L}(X \mid S = s)$ by the empirical quantiles $Q_s = \hat F_s^{-1}$ (sorting, prop. 2.6).
2.  Form the **barycenter** of the $\mu_s$ weighted by the proportions $p_s = \mathbb{P}(S = s)$; in 1D, corollary 2.8 gives its quantile function pointwise: $$Q^\star(u) \;=\; \sum_s\ p_s\, Q_s(u).$$
3.  **Repair**: replace each observation by its counterpart at the same quantile level in the barycenter: $\tilde X_i = Q^\star\big(\hat F_s(X_i)\big)$ for $S_i = s$. In the multivariate case, replace the 1D transport by a Sinkhorn plan between each cloud and a common entropic barycenter (def. 4.3), then use the barycentric projection of the OTDA algorithm (ch. 4).
4.  Retrain the model on the $(\tilde X_i, Y_i)$ *without* the sensitive attribute.

::: proof
*Full repair guarantees demographic parity.* Let $U_s = \hat F_s(X)$ for $X \sim \mu_s$: $U_s$ is (asymptotically) uniform on $[0,1]$, and $\tilde X = Q^\star(U_s)$. Hence the conditional law
$$
\mathcal{L}(\tilde X \mid S = s) = \mathcal{L}\big(Q^\star(U)\big)
$$
*is the same law for every $s$* — the barycenter.

Identical conditionals give independence:
$$
\mathbb{P}(\tilde X \in A, S = s) = \mathbb{P}(\tilde X \in A \mid S = s)\, \mathbb{P}(S = s) = \mathbb{P}(\tilde X \in A)\,\mathbb{P}(S = s).
$$
Any predictor $h(\tilde X)$ then inherits independence from $S$: DP, regardless of the downstream classifier.[∎]{.qed}
:::

**Partial repair**: interpolate the quantiles,
$$
\tilde X^{(\lambda)} = (1-\lambda)\, Q_s(U_s) + \lambda\, Q^\star(U_s),
$$
with $\lambda \in [0, 1]$ — $\lambda = 0$: untouched data; $\lambda = 1$: full repair.

**Utility/fairness trade-off**: as $\lambda$ is swept, the demographic parity gap decreases (the conditionals get closer in Wasserstein distance, linearly in $\lambda$ for the interpolated transport), while accuracy decreases all the faster as $X$ carries signal *correlated* with $S$.

The curve (DP gap on the x-axis, accuracy on the y-axis) is typically decreasing with a "knee" — one chooses $\lambda$ at the elbow, where a lot of equity has been bought for little utility. This is the curve plotted in the lab below.
::::

:::: thm
[Proposition 6.3 — Bicausal OT, counterfactuals and optimal EO post-processing by coupling (simple case proved)]{.tag} **Bicausal OT.** To compare two "twin" individuals differing only in the sensitive attribute, we couple the *joint* laws $\mathcal{L}(S, X)$ with a plan $\pi$ *respecting the causal structure $S \to X$*. This is a **bicausal** coupling: the copy of $X$ depends on the copy of $S$ only through the coupling of the conditionals $\mathcal{L}(X \mid S = s)$ (de Lara, González-Sanz, Asher, Risser & Loubes, JMLR 2024).

The **counterfactual** $X^\star(s')$ — "the value $X$ would have taken had $S$ been $s'$" — is the coupled point: constructed by OT between $\mathcal{L}(X \mid S = s)$ and $\mathcal{L}(X \mid S = s')$.

Applications: measuring discrimination $\mathbb{E}\big[c(X, X^\star)\big]$, predicting on the counterfactual ("counterfactual" fairness).

::: proof
*EO post-processing: the optimal coupling is the increasing coupling.* Simple setting: $Y \in \{0,1\}$, real score $R_s = f(X)$ per group, and a *randomized* post-processing $\hat Y_s = g_s(R_s, U)$, $U \sim \mathcal{U}[0,1]$ common.

1.  Such a post-processing is exactly a **coupling** between the law of $R_s \mid Y = y$ and a target Bernoulli law — the noise $U$ realizes the plan.
2.  EO requires that the law of $\hat Y_s \mid Y = y$ be the same for both groups: we therefore couple *simultaneously* the two conditional score laws to a common target.
3.  Among these couplings, the one maximizing utility (accuracy, increasing in the score within each class) is the **increasing coupling** — quantile matching. The *uncrossing* argument of the proof of prop. 2.6 applies word for word: uncrossing two pairs (making the coupling more comonotone) cannot decrease a utility that is increasing in both scores.

Concretely: bring each score to its rank $U_s = \hat F_s(R_s)$ (quantile within its group), then apply the *same* decision rule to the $U_s$ — the equalization of the conditional laws happens on the quantiles. Choosing the common operating point (TPR, FPR) maximizes the linear utility
$$
\mathbb{P}(Y{=}1)\,\mathrm{TPR} + \mathbb{P}(Y{=}0)\,(1 - \mathrm{FPR})
$$
over the feasible set (the intersection of the two regions convexified by randomization — the "mixture of predictors" procedure of Hardt et al., reread as an OT coupling).[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[Limits and debate: incompatible metrics, utility, causal assumptions]{.tag}

-   **Theoretical incompatibilities**: when the base rates $\mathbb{P}(Y = 1 \mid S = s)$ differ across groups, calibration *and* equalized odds are mutually exclusive (Kleinberg, Mullainathan & Raghavan 2016; Chouldechova 2017): no method — OT included — can satisfy all the criteria; choosing the metric is choosing the trade-off.
-   **Utility cost**: DP repair can destroy a legitimate signal (if $S$ genuinely predicts $Y$, independence forces a loss); "blind" repair is not always fair in the individual sense.
-   **Causal assumptions**: counterfactuals by bicausal OT assume a structure $S \to X$ and the absence of unmeasured confounding; two different optimal bicausal couplings (non-uniqueness, cf. example 1.2) can yield different counterfactuals — OT provides a *family* of models, to be audited (the JMLR 2024 paper proposes statistical tests).
-   **Position of the course**: OT is not an answer to the question of justice, but a *geometric language* for quantifying trade-offs: distances between groups, barycenters, optimal couplings — the same objects as in ch. 1-5.
:::

::: ex
[Guided lab — repair and trade-off curves on Adult (UCI)]{.tag}

```python
import numpy as np, ot
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
# Adult: X = numerical variables, S = gender, Y = income > 50k
# (load with pandas.read_csv("adult.data"), encode the categoricals)

def repair_1d(x, s, lam):
    """Partial quantile repair, feature by feature (th. 6.2)."""
    xR = x.copy()
    qs = {sv: np.sort(x[s == sv]) for sv in np.unique(s)}
    n = min(len(v) for v in qs.values())          # common ranks
    bary = np.mean([v[np.linspace(0, len(v)-1, n).astype(int)]
                    for v in qs.values()], axis=0)  # Q*: average of the quantiles
    for sv in np.unique(s):
        v, idx = np.sort(x[s == sv]), np.argsort(x[s == sv])
        ranks = np.linspace(0, len(v)-1, n)
        rep = (1-lam) * np.interp(ranks, range(len(v)), v) + lam * bary
        xR[s == sv] = np.interp(np.argsort(np.argsort(x[s == sv])),
                                ranks, rep)[np.argsort(idx)]
    return xR

for lam in np.linspace(0, 1, 11):                  # lambda -> trade-off curve
    Xr = repair_1d(X_num, S, lam)
    clf = LogisticRegression().fit(Xr, Y)
    acc = clf.score(Xr, Y)
    dp = abs(clf.predict_proba(Xr[S==0])[:,1].mean()
           - clf.predict_proba(Xr[S==1])[:,1].mean())
    print(f"lambda={lam:.1f}  accuracy={acc:.3f}  dp_gap={dp:.3f}")
# Plot accuracy vs dp_gap: knee of the curve, discussion in the lab
```

Lab questions:

1.  where is the knee, and what does it say?
2.  compare marginal 1D repair and multivariate repair by Sinkhorn;
3.  also measure the EO gap before/after;
4.  does repair preserve calibration? (connect to the debate above).
:::

## 7. Research at CMAP (Flamary, Gaucher) {#ch7}

::: note
[Who teaches this module, and why these chapters]{.tag} Rémi Flamary (CNRS, CMAP, École Polytechnique) is co-director of the LLGA master's program and co-creator of the [POT](https://pythonot.github.io) library. The methods presented in this module — OT domain adaptation (ch. 4), Gromov-Wasserstein and FGW (ch. 5) — partly come from his own papers: this chapter presents them as published, with their links. All the references below are real and verifiable.
:::

::: thm
[POT — Python Optimal Transport (Flamary et al., JMLR 2021): the library of the course]{.tag} [POT: Python Optimal Transport](https://jmlr.org/papers/v22/20-451.html), Journal of Machine Learning Research 22(78), 2021 — [pythonot.github.io](https://pythonot.github.io). **Principle**: a unified library of OT solvers, with an API with three inputs (measures, costs, solver):

-   **Exact solvers**: `ot.emd`, `ot.emd2` (network simplex, ch. 1); 1D by quantiles (`ot.wasserstein_1d`);
-   **Regularized**: `ot.sinkhorn`, `ot.sinkhorn_log` (ch. 3), debiased divergences `ot.sinkhorn_divergence`; exact and entropic barycenters (ch. 4);
-   **Structured**: `ot.gromov` — GW, FGW, COOT (ch. 5); Gaussian (`ot.gaussian.wass2`, th. 2.7); sliced;
-   **Application**: `ot.da` — the transporter of the OTDA algorithm of ch. 4, packaged with label propagation and out-of-sample.

**Result**: some sixty solvers drawn from the literature, NumPy/PyTorch/JAX backends (differentiation of the potential, th. 3.4), an example gallery — the reference tool for numerical OT, used from medical applications to generative AI. **Positioning**: all the labs of this module use it; the architecture of ch. 3 (solvers, regularization, GPU) is exactly its architecture.
:::

::: thm
[Optimal Transport for Domain Adaptation (Courty, Flamary, Tuia & Rakotomamonjy, IEEE TPAMI 2016)]{.tag} [Optimal Transport for Domain Adaptation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1507.00504), IEEE Transactions on Pattern Analysis and Machine Intelligence 39(9), 2016.

**Principle**: that of the OTDA algorithm of ch. 4 — regularized coupling (entropy + *class regularization* by group-lasso) between the source/target clouds, barycentric transport of the labeled points, learning in the target space.

**Result**: theory (error bounds linking the source-target Wasserstein distance and the target risk) and experimental gains on images and texts; the extension [JDOT](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.08848) (Courty, Flamary, Habrard & Rakotomamonjy, NeurIPS 2017) transports the joint law $(X, Y)$ by including the label loss in the cost — the direct ancestor of OT training losses.

**Positioning**: this is ch. 4 of the course; the modern benchmark SKADA-Bench (TMLR 2025) measures its successors.
:::

::: thm
[Fused Gromov-Wasserstein (Vayer, Chapel, Flamary, Tavenard & Courty, ICML 2019)]{.tag} [Optimal Transport for structured data with application on graphs](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v97/titouan19a.html), ICML 2019 (PMLR 97).

**Principle**: the FGW distance of ch. 5 — combining the *feature* cost and the *structure* cost under a parameter $\alpha$, with continuity and bounds with respect to the two extremes; a linearization-type algorithm (PGW).

**Result**: classification and *barycenters* of attributed graphs (the "average" of several graphs exists: it is used in classification by nearest barycenter); applications to molecules/time series.

**Positioning**: def. 5.3 of the course; the "graphs" side extends into M1P2 (Graph ML module, ch. 5 and 9) and up to FGW-template GNNs (NeurIPS 2022).
:::

::: thm
[CO-Optimal Transport (Redko, Vayer, Flamary & Courty, NeurIPS 2020)]{.tag} [CO-Optimal Transport](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.03731), NeurIPS 2020 — code [github.com/PythonOT/COOT](https://github.com/PythonOT/COOT).

**Principle**: def. 5.4 — transporting *simultaneously* the samples (rows) and the variables (columns) of two data matrices via two alternating couplings.

**Result**: a unifying framework subsuming OT, GW and co-clustering; marked gains in *heterogeneous* domain adaptation (datasets with different features: texts in different languages, distinct sensors).

**Positioning**: the "double alternation" of ch. 5; available in POT (`ot.gromov.co_optimal_transport`).
:::

::: note
[Two recent tracks: sliced under the magnifier, OT for biosignals]{.tag}

-   **Sliced theory**: E. Tanguy, R. Flamary & J. Delon, [Reconstructing discrete measures from projections. Consequences on the empirical Sliced Wasserstein Distance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.12029), Comptes Rendus Mathématique 362, 2024 — which projections determine a discrete measure, and what this implies for the empirical sliced distance (def. 3.5): the $n^{-1/2}$ rate of th. 4.5 is dissected there. **Positioning**: the fine analysis of the favorite estimator of high-dimensional ML.
-   **OT and physiological signals**: T. Gnassounou, R. Flamary & A. Gramfort, [Convolutional Monge Mapping Normalization for learning on biosignals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18831), NeurIPS 2023 — normalizing each subject's EEG *toward a common Wasserstein barycenter* (def. 4.3) via a convolutional map: clear gains in brain decoding. **Positioning**: the exact bridge between this module and the Signal Processing module M1P1 (ch. 9): spectra, transport, normalization.
:::

## Exercises {#ex}

1.  **★ Duality in dimension 2 (solution).** Source and target in $\mathbb{R}$, cost $\|x - y\|$:
    $$
    a = (1/2, 1/2) \text{ at } x_1 = 0,\ x_2 = 1, \qquad b = (1/2, 1/2) \text{ at } y_1 = 0,\ y_2 = 2.
    $$
    Write the primal, guess the optimal plan, deduce the dual potentials from the complementarity of th. 2.1 and check the equality of the values.

    *Solution (sketch).* The cost matrix is $C = \begin{pmatrix}0 & 2\\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, and the extreme admissible plans are
    $$
    \Gamma_1 = \big(\begin{smallmatrix}1/2 & 0\\ 0 & 1/2\end{smallmatrix}\big) \ (\text{cost } 1/2), \qquad \Gamma_2 = \big(\begin{smallmatrix}0 & 1/2\\ 1/2 & 0\end{smallmatrix}\big) \ (\text{cost } 3/2).
    $$
    Optimum: $\Gamma_1$, with $W_1 = 1/2$.

    Complementarity: the support of $\Gamma^\star$ is $\{(1,1), (2,2)\}$, which gives the equalities $f_1 + g_1 = C_{11} = 0$ and $f_2 + g_2 = C_{22} = 1$, together with the inequalities $f_1 + g_2 \leq 2$ and $f_2 + g_1 \leq 1$.

    Take $f = (0, 1)$, $g = (0, 0)$: the value $\langle a, f\rangle + \langle b, g\rangle = 1/2$ equals the primal value — strong duality verified by hand.
2.  **★ Sinkhorn 2×2 by hand (solution).** With $a = b = (1/2, 1/2)$, $C = \begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\ 1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ and $\varepsilon = 1$, compute $K$ and initialize $v = \mathbf{1}$. Then perform two complete iterations of
    $$
    u \leftarrow a/(Kv), \qquad v \leftarrow b/(K^\top u),
    $$
    and check that the row marginals converge to $a$.

    *Solution (values).* The kernel is
    $$
    K = \big(\begin{smallmatrix}1 & e^{-1}\\ e^{-1} & 1\end{smallmatrix}\big).
    $$
    Iteration 1: $Kv = (1 + e^{-1}, 1 + e^{-1})^\top$, so $u = \frac{1}{2(1+e^{-1})}(1,1)^\top$; then $K^\top u = \frac12(1,1)^\top$, so $v = (1,1)^\top$ again. The second iteration reproduces the same $u$ and $v$: the fixed point is reached after a single complete iteration (symmetric case).

    The plan
    $$
    \Gamma = \mathrm{diag}(u)\,K = \frac{1}{2(1+e^{-1})}\big(\begin{smallmatrix}1 & e^{-1}\\ e^{-1} & 1\end{smallmatrix}\big) \approx \big(\begin{smallmatrix}0.366 & 0.134\\ 0.134 & 0.366\end{smallmatrix}\big)
    $$
    indeed has rows and columns summing to $1/2$; the entropic plan "blurs" the diagonal toward the anti-diagonal (entropic bias, ch. 3).
3.  **★ Bures in simulation (lab).** Draw $n = 5000$ points from two anisotropic 2D Gaussians ($\Sigma_1 = \mathrm{diag}(4, 1)$ rotated, $\Sigma_2 = \mathrm{diag}(1, 4)$), compare the empirical $W_2^2$ (Sinkhorn on the samples) with the closed formula of th. 2.7 and with `ot.gaussian.wass2`. Observe the effect of $\varepsilon$.

    *Hint.* The gap comes from the entropic bias (use `ot.sinkhorn_divergence`) and from the sampling noise ($n^{-1/d}$, th. 4.5: severe in dimension 2 if $n$ is small).
4.  **★ Weighted Gaussian barycenter (hint).** Rederive corollary 2.8 with arbitrary weights, then in the case of two laws $\mathcal{N}(0, 1)$ and $\mathcal{N}(0, 9)$: show that the standard deviation of the equal-weight barycenter equals $2$ (and not $\sqrt{5}$), and comment ("the mean of the variances" is not the barycenter).

    *Hint.* Minimize pointwise in $u$ the quantile function (zero derivative), then identify the resulting Gaussian quantile: $\sigma = \sum_k w_k \sigma_k$.
5.  **★ WMD on two sentences (solution).** With real word2vec embeddings (Text Mining and NLP module, ch. 4), compute the WMD between "the president addresses the congress" and "Obama speaks to the parliament", then between two unrelated sentences; display the plan (`ot.emd`) and comment on the word matchings.

    *Solution (key).* Documents = uniform distributions over the words (minus the stopwords); cost = Euclidean distance between embeddings (not its square: WMD uses $W_1$); the plan connects "president"↔"Obama", "congress"↔"parliament" (neighbors in the space): the distance stays small where the centroid distance would be misled by function words.
6.  **★ GW invariant, W not (solution).** Let $\mu$ be uniform on three non-collinear points of the plane and $\nu = \tau_\#\mu$ its translate by a vector of norm $r$, with the internal Euclidean distances. Show $\mathrm{GW}_2(\mu, \nu) = 0$ and $W_2(\mu, \nu) = r$. What happens under a rotation?

    *Solution.* The translation $\tau$ preserves all the internal distances (an isometry in the sense of th. 5.2): diagonal plan at zero cost. For $W_2$, the plan $(\mathrm{Id}, \tau)_\#\mu$ costs
    $$
    \big(\int \|x - (x + \tau)\|^2 d\mu\big)^{1/2} = r,
    $$
    and no coupling can do better, since by Jensen
    $$
    \mathbb{E}\|X - Y\|^2 \geq \|\mathbb{E}X - \mathbb{E}Y\|^2 = r^2
    $$
    for every coupling $(X, Y)$ (the means differ by the translation).

    Rotation: still GW = 0 (isometry); $W_2 > 0$ as soon as the points actually move — this is the motivation of ch. 5 (objects defined up to an isometry).
7.  **★★ Kantorovich-Rubinstein (solution).** In the framework of prop. 4.2, show that if $f$ is 1-Lipschitz then $f^c = -f$ for the cost $c(x, y) = |x - y|$ (in dimension 1), and conclude that
    $$
    W_1(\mu, \nu) = \sup_{\mathrm{Lip}(f) \leq 1} \int f\,d(\mu - \nu).
    $$

    *Solution (key).* By definition,
    $$
    f^c(y) = \inf_x [|x - y| - f(x)].
    $$
    The choice $x = y$ gives $f^c(y) \leq -f(y)$. For every $x$, $f(x) \leq f(y) + |x - y|$ (1-Lipschitz), hence
    $$
    |x - y| - f(x) \geq -f(y) .
    $$
    The infimum is therefore attained at $x = y$, and $f^c = -f$. The dual of th. 2.1 becomes $\int f\,d\mu + \int (-f)\,d\nu$ over the admissible pairs $(f, -f)$, which are exactly (up to an additive constant) the 1-Lipschitz functions — hence the formula.
8.  **★★ Vertices of the transport polytope (solution) — promised in ch. 1.** Show that an optimal plan can be chosen with at most $n + m - 1$ non-zero coefficients (th. 1.3), build an example where the optimal plan is *not* deterministic, and connect it to example 1.2.

    *Solution (sketch).* Vertex: $nm$ variables, constraints of rank $\leq n + m - 1$ (sum of the rows = sum of the columns); a vertex requires $nm$ independent active constraints, of which at least $nm - (n+m-1)$ are $\Gamma_{ij} = 0$.

    Non-deterministic example: $a = (1)$ at $x_1$, $b = (1/2, 1/2)$ — every plan has the form $(1/2, 1/2)$, one row toward two columns: no vertex is a partial permutation. Link: this is example 1.2 (one mass, two half-masses).

    In general, a vertex has at most $n + m - 1$ non-zeros spread over $n$ rows, each row having at least one: at most $m - 1$ rows carry more than one non-zero, so when $n \gg m$ almost every source point goes to a single target.

    And when $n = m$ with uniform weights $1/n$, Birkhoff's theorem says that the vertices are permutation matrices divided by $n$ — the optimal plan is then a map.
9.  **★★ Partial repair and repair speed (hint).** In the 1D framework of th. 6.2, show that the level-$\lambda$ partial repair sends the conditionals toward laws at distance
    $$
    W_2\big(\mathcal{L}(\tilde X^{(\lambda)}\mid S{=}0), \mathcal{L}(\tilde X^{(\lambda)}\mid S{=}1)\big) = (1-\lambda)\, W_2(\mu_0, \mu_1).
    $$

    *Hint.* Write the interpolated quantile functions $Q^{(\lambda)}_s = (1-\lambda)Q_s + \lambda Q^\star$ and use prop. 2.6: the difference factorizes,
    $$
    Q^{(\lambda)}_0(u) - Q^{(\lambda)}_1(u) = (1-\lambda)(Q_0(u) - Q_1(u)).
    $$
10. **★★ Limits of FGW (hint).** Check that $\mathrm{FGW}_{\alpha=1}$ recovers the OT of the features and $\mathrm{FGW}_{\alpha=0}$ pure GW, then build two graphs where the FGW ranking changes from one to the other (consistent features but opposite structures).

    *Hint.* Take two 3-node graphs: the same star; features swapped between center and leaves; plot FGW as a function of $\alpha$ (continuity, def. 5.3) on a synthetic set in POT.
11. **★★ Binary equalized odds (hint).** Two groups of equal sizes, $Y$ binary and balanced within each, perfect scores for group 0 ($\hat Y = Y$) and random scores (coin flips) for group 1. Determine the randomized post-processing of prop. 6.3 that achieves EO, and its accuracy.

    *Hint.* In ROC coordinates (FPR, TPR), randomization makes the feasible set of each group convex: for group 0 (perfect scores) it is the triangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(0,1)$, $(1,1)$; for group 1 (coin flips) it is only the diagonal $\mathrm{TPR} = \mathrm{FPR}$.

    EO forces a common point, hence a point of the diagonal, where (balanced classes) the accuracy in both groups is
    $$
    \tfrac12\mathrm{TPR} + \tfrac12(1 - \mathrm{FPR}) = \tfrac12 .
    $$
    Group 0 must be "noised" down to chance level. Discuss this cost (the debate of ch. 6).
12. **★★★ Synthesis lab — OTDA + FGW in POT.** (a) Generate two 2D "source/target" clouds (shifted moons): full OTDA of ch. 4 with `ot.da.SinkhornLpl1Transport` (class-regularized transport, then `transform`), accuracy before/after.

    (b) Two attributed 15-node graphs (stochastic block models): FGW alignment (`ot.gromov.fused_gromov_wasserstein`), recovered permutation matrix (f-score); sweep $\alpha$ and $\varepsilon$, multiple initializations (GW non-convex, th. 5.2).

    Deliverables: curves, transport plan visualized (`ot.plot.plot1D_mat`), a short analysis.
